# Module 1: Oncogenes

| Gene | Biological role |
|---|---|
| TP53 | Tumor suppressor, DNA damage response |
| KRAS | Oncogene, MAPK signaling |
| BRAF | Oncogene, MAPK signaling |
| APC | Tumor suppressor, WNT signaling |
| PTEN | Tumor suppressor, PI3K/AKT signaling |
| PIK3CA | Oncogene, PI3K signaling |
| EGFR | Receptor tyrosine kinase |
| RB1 | Tumor suppressor, cell-cycle regulation |
| CDKN2A | Tumor suppressor, cell-cycle control |
| SMARCA4 | Chromatin remodeling |


# Task 1: Oncogenes

`oncogenes` contains a set of ten genes that are strongly associated with tomorigenesis and therefore highly clinically relevant. 

```{r}
oncogenes
```



1.2 How many cell lines show a mutation for each of the oncogenes. What is the most frequently mutated oncogene?

```{r}
mut[HugoSymbol %in% oncogenes, .N, by = HugoSymbol][order(-N)]
```

# 1.2: Find out the mean expression of SOX10 in Melanoma cell lines, as well as in non-Melanoma cell lines. 

```{r}
cell_lines_oi <- models[OncotreePrimaryDisease == "Melanoma", unique(ModelID)]

mean(expression[setdiff(rownames(expression), cell_lines_oi),"SOX10"], na.rm = T)
mean(expression[intersect(rownames(expression), cell_lines_oi),"SOX10"], na.rm = T)

```


# 1.3: Tumors can be caused by different kinds of mutations. Popular tumor-causing mutations are loss of function of tumor suppressor genes. Compute the number of mutations per oncogene, now also including if the mutation is likely a loss of function mutation. Find a way to plot these numbers. Do you observe a difference for TP53 and KRAS?

```{r}
mut[HugoSymbol %in% oncogenes, .N, by = .(HugoSymbol, LikelyLoF)] |>
  ggplot(aes(N, HugoSymbol, fill = LikelyLoF)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
